title: Derived mapping spaces under a cofibrant base
statement:
Use model categories, cofibrant and fibrant objects, cosimplicial frames, homotopy coherent localizations and their mapping spaces of [lem-coef-cosimplicial-frame-mapping], and homotopy fibers of Kan complexes of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $\mathcal M$ be a model category with functorial factorizations, $O$ a cofibrant object, $i:O\to C$ a cofibration and $f:O\to Y$ a map with $Y$ fibrant. The ordinary category $O\downarrow\mathcal M$ has objects maps from $O$ and morphisms commuting strictly with those maps. It has the model structure whose weak equivalences, cofibrations and fibrations are the underlying ones in $\mathcal M$. Write $\operatorname{Map}^h$ for the mapping space in the respective homotopy coherent localization, computed by frames. Forgetting the maps from $O$, with their specified equality, induces a natural equivalence
$$\operatorname{Map}^h_{O\downarrow\mathcal M}(i,f)\simeq\operatorname{hofib}_f\bigl(\operatorname{Map}^h_{\mathcal M}(C,Y)\xrightarrow{i^*}\operatorname{Map}^h_{\mathcal M}(O,Y)\bigr).$$
The comparison retains the path to $f$ and its higher simplices. It is coherently natural for precomposition by maps of cofibrant objects under $O$ and postcomposition by maps of fibrant objects under $O$. No simplicial enrichment, properness or combinatorial hypothesis on $\mathcal M$ is imposed.

source.place: Hovey Proposition 1.1.8 and the paragraph immediately after its proof, printed p.5, for the undercategory model structure; Sections 5.2 and 5.4 for compatible frames and relative function complexes. The displayed homotopy-fiber comparison is an agent-formulated relative-frame consequence, not a verbatim theorem of Hovey. WANTED: archived Hovey and an explicit published relative function-complex reference; no Stacks tag states this infinity-localization assertion.

proof.text: Write $\mathcal U=O\downarrow\mathcal M$. Limits in $\mathcal U$ are computed by taking the limit of the underlying diagram in $\mathcal M$ and using the compatible maps from $O$; a cone under $O$ is then exactly a cone to that limit. Colimits are computed by taking the colimit $T$ of the underlying objects and pushing out the induced map from the colimit of the constant $O$-diagram along its canonical map to $O$. The universal property of this pushout identifies maps under $O$ with the required cocones, including the empty diagram. Thus $\mathcal U$ is complete and cocomplete, with initial object $1_O:O\to O$ and terminal object $O\to 1$.

Declare a morphism in $\mathcal U$ to be a weak equivalence, cofibration or fibration exactly when its underlying morphism in $\mathcal M$ is one. Two-out-of-three and retract closure are inherited. Factor an underlying arrow functorially in either of the two weak factorization systems of $\mathcal M$ and give the middle object the composite map from $O$; both factors then commute with the structure maps. Any lifting problem in $\mathcal U$ is the same underlying lifting problem in $\mathcal M$, and a ground-category filler automatically commutes with $O$. Conversely, if an under-arrow lifts against every map in the opposite class, lifting against its chosen factorization exhibits it as an arrow retract of the corresponding factor, so the lifting classes are exact. Hence these classes form the two functorial weak factorization systems and give the asserted model structure.

The initial map of $i$ in $\mathcal U$ is the underlying cofibration $i:O\to C$, and the terminal map of $f$ is $Y\to1$. Thus $i$ is cofibrant in $\mathcal U$ and $f$ is fibrant there. Also $C$ is cofibrant in $\mathcal M$: its initial map is the composite $0\to O\to C$ of cofibrations. These are distinct cofibrancy assertions; no assertion is made that forgetting a $\mathcal U$-frame yields a frame in $\mathcal M$.

source.place: Proposition 1.1.8; definitions of cofibrant and fibrant objects

proof.text: Choose a frame $A^\bullet\xrightarrow{a}\operatorname{const}O$ in $\mathcal M$, with $A^0=O$ and $a^0=1_O$. Apply the Reedy factorization-extension theorem to $i a:A^\bullet\to\operatorname{const}C$, keeping its degree-zero factorization $O\xrightarrow{i}C\xrightarrow{1_C}C$. It gives $A^\bullet\xrightarrow{u}B^\bullet\xrightarrow{b}\operatorname{const}C$, where $u$ is a Reedy cofibration, $b$ a Reedy trivial fibration, $u^0=i$, and $b^0=1_C$. The starting factorization is in the required two classes because $i$ is a cofibration and $1_C$ is a trivial fibration. Since $A^\bullet$ is Reedy cofibrant, composition of cofibrations in the Reedy model category makes $B^\bullet$ Reedy cofibrant. Since $b$ is objectwise a weak equivalence, $B^\bullet$ is a frame on $C$ in $\mathcal M$. Functorial degree extensions can be used with the frame on $O$ fixed.

source.place: Theorem 5.2.5, Remark 5.2.3 and the fixed-degree-zero construction in Theorem 5.2.8; compatible source-frame construction

proof.text: Form the cosimplicial object $D^n=B^n\amalg_{A^n}O$ under $O$, using $u^n$ and $a^n$; its augmentation $d:D^\bullet\to\operatorname{const}(i)$ comes from $b$ and $i$. At degree zero $D^0=C\amalg_O O\cong C$, with $d^0=1_C$. To check latching cofibrancy in $\mathcal U$, put $P_n=A^n\amalg_{L_nA}L_nB$. The universal property of colimits and pushouts gives the underlying object of $L_n^{\mathcal U}D$ as $O\amalg_{L_nA}L_nB$. Its map to $D^n$ is the pushout of the relative latching cofibration $P_n\to B^n$ along $P_n\to O\amalg_{L_nA}L_nB$. Hence it is a cofibration. This formula also holds for $n=0$, where it is $O\to C$. It uses colimits in $\mathcal U$, rather than the latching objects of the underlying $D^\bullet$ in $\mathcal M$.

source.place: Definition 5.2.7; relative latching and pushout universal properties; agent expansion for the undercategory

proof.text: For each $n$, all of $A^n,B^n,O$ are cofibrant, and $u^n:A^n\to B^n$ is a cofibration, by the objectwise consequences of the Reedy theorem. Apply clause (b) of the cofibrant-colimit gluing lemma to the map of spans $(A^n\leftarrow A^n\xrightarrow{u^n}B^n)\to(O\xleftarrow{a^n}A^n\xrightarrow{u^n}B^n)$ with components $(a^n,1,1)$. Both right-hand span maps are $u^n$, so the gluing hypotheses hold without left properness. The induced map $B^n\to D^n$ is a weak equivalence. Its composite with $d^n$ is $b^n$, also a weak equivalence; two-out-of-three gives $d^n$ a weak equivalence. Together with the preceding latching calculation and $d^0=1_C$, this proves that $D^\bullet$ is a frame on $i$ in $\mathcal U$.

source.place: Lemma 5.2.6 (cube lemma), applied to the displayed cofibrant spans; Definition 5.2.7 in the undercategory

proof.text: Let $E=H(B^\bullet,Y)$ and $K=H(A^\bullet,Y)$, with restriction $p:E\to K$. The actual map $f:O\to Y$ defines a vertex of $K$ because $A^0=O$; its degenerate $n$-simplex is the map $f a^n:A^n\to Y$. By the pushout universal property, a map $D^n\to Y$ under $O$ is exactly a map $h:B^n\to Y$ satisfying $h u^n=f a^n$. Therefore $$H_{\mathcal U}(D^\bullet,f)\cong E\times_{K}\{f\}.$$ The bijections commute with every simplex operator because all maps come from the same cosimplicial pushout. In particular the required equation is over $A^n$ with right-hand side $f a^n$, not an equation over an unspecified constant base frame.

source.place: Section 5.4 function complexes; degreewise pushout universal property, agent relative-frame calculation

proof.text: The source-restriction lemma applies to the Reedy cofibration $u:A^\bullet\to B^\bullet$ of frames on the cofibrant objects $O,C$ and the fibrant target $Y$. Thus $p:E\to K$ is a Kan fibration of Kan complexes. The strict-pullback clause of the frame-mapping theorem identifies $E\times_K\{f\}$ with the homotopy pullback, hence with $\operatorname{hofib}_f(p)$. In the explicit path model the comparison sends a strict fiber simplex to itself together with the constant path at the corresponding simplex of $f$; this comparison is an equivalence, rather than a claim that every homotopy-fiber path is literally constant.

source.place: Proposition 5.4.3, adjointed against Y→1; strict-pullback comparison as cited in lem-coef-cosimplicial-frame-mapping

proof.text: Apply the frame mapping-space theorem in $\mathcal M$ to $B^\bullet,C,Y$ and to $A^\bullet,O,Y$, and separately in $\mathcal U$ to $D^\bullet,i,f$. It identifies $E,K,H_{\mathcal U}(D^\bullet,f)$ with the three required derived mapping spaces. The augmented map $u$ covers $i$ and the vertex of $K$ is the actual map $f$; naturality of the frame identifications therefore makes $p$ represent $i^*$. The forgetful functor $\mathcal U\to\mathcal M$ is not left Quillen, so it is handled through its left adjoint $F(X)=(O\to O\amalg X)$: $F(g)$ is a pushout of $g$, so $F$ preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations, and the forgetful functor preserves all weak equivalences. The derived adjunction gives $\operatorname{Map}^h_{\mathcal U}(FC,f)\simeq\operatorname{Map}^h_{\mathcal M}(C,Y)$; by the triangle identity, precomposition with the counit $\varepsilon=(i,1_C):FC\to i$ followed by it is the forgetful map. By the left-Quillen clause of the frame theorem, $FB^\bullet$ is a $\mathcal U$-frame on $FC$ and $H_{\mathcal U}(FB^\bullet,f)=E$ degreewise realizes that equivalence. The maps $O\amalg B^n\to D^n$ (structure map and $B^n\to D^n$) form a map of $\mathcal U$-frames $FB^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ with degree-zero component $\varepsilon$, compatible with the augmentations since $d^n$ restricts to $i$ and $b^n$. Frame naturality in $\mathcal U$ thus makes restriction along $B^n\to D^n$ represent the forgetful map: this is forgetting the under-map and its specified equality. Combining the strict-fiber isomorphism and the homotopy-pullback equivalence proves the displayed equivalence, retaining the full homotopy fiber with all higher simplices.

source.place: Corollary 5.4.4 and Proposition 5.4.7, with the localization comparison already stated in lem-coef-cosimplicial-frame-mapping

proof.text: Use the fixed $A^\bullet$ and the functorial relative factorization of Step 4 for every cofibration $O\to C$. A map $g:C\to C^{\prime}$ under $O$ induces $B^\bullet\to B^{\prime\bullet}$ over $g$ and the identity of $A^\bullet$, hence a map $D^\bullet\to D^{\prime\bullet}$. Postcomposition by a map $Y\to Y^{\prime}$ under $O$ sends $f a^n$ to $f^{\prime}a^n$. Thus the strict-fiber isomorphisms and the comparisons to path fibers are natural maps of simplicial sets, with composition and identities inherited from the functorial choices. The naturality in the homotopy theory of both inputs supplied by the frame theorem identifies these transformations with precomposition and postcomposition on derived mapping spaces, including their coherent simplices. This proves the stated coherent naturality. None of these steps imposes enrichment, properness or combinatoriality.

source.place: Theorem 5.2.8, functorial relative Reedy extensions; Sections 5.4 and 5.6, through the naturality interface of the cited frame-mapping theorem
